sketches.title: Clue Under Clue
sketches.premise: A treasure hunt has begun, and one more clue appears after each clue is followed. Take turns explaining what the new clue makes the hunters do next. The host will note when your clever plan is merely a plan wearing a hat.
sketches.criterion: A move FOLLOWS when it is one plain, immediate discovery or action caused by the standing clue, uses the whole transcript, adds a usable clue or obstacle, and does not skip from clue to treasure, declare the hunt over, undo a discovery, repeat the same clue, or introduce a stranger the hunt could not have reached.
sketches.move_shape: Write one event beginning with “Then,” naming the new clue and the one action it causes; for example: “Then the muddy boot print points them to the shed, where a brass key is tucked under the third flowerpot.”
sketches.first_card: A map fragment is found inside a library book; its only mark is a blue circle around the word “clock.”

sketches.title: The Hostile Map
sketches.premise: Two hunters share a map that keeps revealing one more marked place. Each turn, say how the current mark leads the hunters to the next mark. The map is not evil; it is simply committed to making ordinary walking inconvenient.
sketches.criterion: A move FOLLOWS when one visible map mark plainly causes one reachable search or discovery that fits every earlier mark, while a skipped journey, a finished treasure find, an erased mark, a duplicate restatement, or a person or place that cannot have entered the hunt fails.
sketches.move_shape: Give one sentence starting “Then the mark sends them…” and name the new place or sign; for example: “Then the mark sends them behind the picnic shelter, where a painted arrow points toward the creek.”
sketches.first_card: The map shows a red square around the town fountain and a tiny line leading away from it.

sketches.title: The Box That Explains Itself
sketches.premise: A locked box is the shared object. Every turn adds one new clue about how to open it, and the next clue must be caused by the last one. You may make the box absurdly fussy, but you may not open it until the chain has earned the lid.
sketches.criterion: A move FOLLOWS when it is one physical clue or test revealed by the standing clue and useful for the next attempt, fits the transcript, and does not jump to the open box, cancel a failed test, repeat a clue, or add an impossible helper or object without a link.
sketches.move_shape: Write “Then the test reveals…” followed by one new detail and its direct use; for example: “Then the three wrong keys leave chalk marks on the lock, showing that the right key must be warm.”
sketches.first_card: A small wooden box sits on a table with three keyholes, one shaped like a leaf.

sketches.title: Trail of Small Errors
sketches.premise: The hunters follow a treasure trail, but each clue sends them into one harmless, growing mistake. Take turns saying what the current mistake causes next, while keeping the clue hunt alive. The host will explain that walking past the sign is not a plot twist.
sketches.criterion: A move FOLLOWS when one new, plain mistake is caused by the standing mistake and changes the hunters’ next clue or location, while a skipped chain, a clean rescue, a reversal, a repeated error, or an unrelated newcomer fails.
sketches.move_shape: Start with “Then,” name one immediate mistake and the new clue it exposes; for example: “Then they read ‘turn left’ upside down, enter the bakery, and find a sugar-covered note under the counter.”
sketches.first_card: The first clue says, “Follow the birds,” and a row of paper birds leads from the park gate.

sketches.title: The Clue Trades Hands
sketches.premise: One treasure clue is passed from person to person as the hunt moves through town. Each turn says who gets it next and what that person notices, so the clue continues its journey. Nobody has to be mysterious; the clue has enough work already.
sketches.criterion: A move FOLLOWS when the standing holder’s action plainly puts the same clue into one new holder’s hands and that holder adds a useful detail, while a skipped handoff, a final treasure claim, taking the clue back, repeating the holder, or adding someone the scene cannot connect fails.
sketches.move_shape: Write “Then [holder] passes it to [new holder], who notices…” and give one new clue detail; for example: “Then Mina passes it to the bus driver, who notices the ink matches the route number for the old mill.”
sketches.first_card: A folded clue slips from a guidebook at the museum and lands beside a janitor’s cart.

sketches.title: The Last Line Moves
sketches.premise: Each treasure clue has a last line that points somewhere, but the next turn must make that line matter in the real world. Follow the changing trail one small result at a time. If you announce the treasure, the host will mark the exciting conclusion and stop the game, which is efficient but not useful.
sketches.criterion: A move FOLLOWS when the last line of the standing clue directly causes one new search, sign, or clue that fits the whole transcript, while a skipped result, an ending, an undo, a duplicate clue, or an impossible new witness fails.
sketches.move_shape: Say “Then the last line leads them to…” and name one place where a new clue is found; for example: “Then the last line leads them to the bus stop, where the route board has one number circled in red.”
sketches.first_card: The first note says, “Where the town rests its feet, look below the oldest number.”
